metadata.title: Theory of Rational Option Pricing
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Assumption 1 (No-dominance principle)
nodes.statement: A necessary condition for a rational option pricing theory is that the option be priced such that it is neither a dominant nor a dominated security.
nodes.statement_clean: A rational option price must be neither dominant nor dominated by any other security.

nodes.name: Assumption 2 (Distribution-only identification)
nodes.statement: If $S_i = S_j$, $\tau_i = \tau_j$, $E_i = E_j$, and the returns per dollar on stocks $i$ and $j$ are identically distributed, then $F_i(S, \tau; E) = F_j(S, \tau; E)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Warrants on stocks with identical return distributions have equal value.

nodes.name: Dominant security
nodes.statement: Security (portfolio) $A$ is dominant over security (portfolio) $B$ if on some known date in the future, the return on $A$ will exceed the return on $B$ for some possible states of the world, and will be at least as large as on $B$ in all possible states of the world.
nodes.statement_clean: A dominates B if A's return matches or beats B's in every state, and strictly exceeds it in at least one.

nodes.name: Warrant / call / put notation
nodes.statement: $F(S,\tau;E)$ is the value of an American warrant with exercise price $E$ and $\tau$ years before expiration when the stock price per share is $S$; $f(S,\tau;E)$ its European counterpart; $G(S,\tau;E)$ the American put; $g(S,\tau;E)$ the European put.
nodes.statement_clean: Notation: F, f, G, g denote American/European warrant and put prices as functions of stock price S, time-to-expiry tau, and exercise price E.

nodes.name: More risky security
nodes.statement: Security one is more risky than security two if $Z_1(\tau) = Z_2(\tau) + \epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is a random variable with $E[\epsilon \mid Z_2(\tau)] = 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Security 1 is riskier than security 2 if its return equals security 2's plus mean-zero noise (Rothschild-Stiglitz mean-preserving spread).

nodes.name: Payout-protected option
nodes.statement: An option is payout protected if, for a fixed investment policy and fixed capital structure, the value of the option is invariant to the choice of payout policy.
nodes.statement_clean: An option is payout protected if its value does not depend on the firm's payout (dividend) policy.

nodes.name: Discount-bond price
nodes.statement: Let $P(\tau)$ be the price of a riskless (in terms of default), discounted loan paying one dollar $\tau$ years from now; $1 = P(0) > P(\tau_1) > \dots > P(\tau_n)$ for $0 < \tau_1 < \dots < \tau_n$ when interest rates are positive.

nodes.name: Down-and-out call option
nodes.statement: A call option with the same terms as the standard call but additionally voided (worthless) if the stock price falls below a stated 'knock-out' level $B(T) = bE \exp[-\eta T]$, $0 < b < 1$, $\eta \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Terminal warrant payoff
nodes.statement_clean: At expiration the warrant pays max(0, S-E).

nodes.name: Arbitrage lower bound on American warrant
nodes.statement: $F(S, \tau; E) \geq \max[0, S - E]$.
nodes.statement_clean: American warrant value is at least its intrinsic value.

nodes.name: Stock-price SDE (geometric Brownian motion)
nodes.statement: $\dfrac{dS}{S} = \alpha\, dt + \sigma\, dz$, where $\alpha$ is the instantaneous expected return, $\sigma^2$ the instantaneous variance, and $dz$ a standard Gauss-Wiener process.
nodes.statement_clean: Stock follows geometric Brownian motion with drift alpha and volatility sigma.

nodes.name: Bond-price SDE
nodes.statement: $\dfrac{dP}{P} = \mu(\tau)\, dt + \delta(\tau)\, dq(t;\tau)$, with cross-maturity correlations $dq(t;\tau)\,dq(t;T) = \rho_{\tau T}\,dt$ and no serial correlation.
nodes.statement_clean: Bond price for maturity tau evolves as an Ito process with drift mu(tau) and volatility delta(tau).

nodes.name: Black-Scholes PDE (Merton form)
nodes.statement: $\tfrac{1}{2}[\sigma^2 S^2 H_{11} + 2\rho\sigma\delta S P H_{12} + \delta^2 P^2 H_{22}] - H_3 = 0$, a second-order linear parabolic PDE for the warrant price $H(S,P,\tau;E)$.
nodes.statement_clean: PDE governing the rational warrant price under stochastic stock and bond dynamics.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes call formula
nodes.statement: $f(S,\tau;E) = S\,\Phi(d_1) - E e^{-r\tau}\,\Phi(d_2)$, where $d_1 = \dfrac{\log(S/E) + (r + \tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}$, $d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{\tau}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Closed-form Black-Scholes price for a European call.

nodes.name: Sufficient condition for no premature exercise (continuous dividend)
nodes.statement: $E > d/r$, the continuous-time analogue of $E > \sum_t d(t) P(\tau-t) / [1 - P(\tau)]$.
nodes.statement_clean: If exercise price exceeds present value of remaining dividends, never exercise early.

nodes.name: Dividend-adjusted warrant PDE
nodes.statement: $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 W_{11} + (rS - D) W_1 - W_2 - rW = 0$, with boundary conditions $W(0,\tau;E)=0$, $W(S,0;E)=\max[0,S-E]$, and the arbitrage bound $W \geq \max[0, S-E]$ for the American case.
nodes.statement_clean: Black-Scholes-type PDE incorporating a continuous dividend stream D(S, tau).

nodes.name: American put PDE
nodes.statement: $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 G_{11} + r S G_1 - r G - G_2 = 0$, subject to $G(\infty,\tau;E)=0$, $G(S,0;E) = \max[0,E-S]$, $G(S,\tau;E) \geq \max[0,E-S]$.

nodes.name: Perpetual American put price
nodes.statement: $G(S,\infty;E) = \dfrac{E}{1+\gamma}\,[(1+\gamma)S/(\gamma E)]^{-\gamma}$, where $\gamma = 2r/\sigma^2$ and the optimal exercise boundary is $C^* = \gamma E/(1+\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Down-and-out call price
nodes.statement: $f(S,T;E) = \tfrac12[S\,\mathrm{erfc}(h_1) - E e^{-rT} \mathrm{erfc}(h_2)] - (S/B[T])^{\delta}\,\tfrac12[B[T]\,\mathrm{erfc}(h_3) - (S/B[T])^{-1} E e^{-rT}\,\mathrm{erfc}(h_4)]$, with $\delta = 2(r-\eta)/\sigma^2$ and $h_i$ defined in the text.
nodes.statement_clean: Closed-form European down-and-out call price, equal to a standard call minus a 'knock-out discount.'

nodes.name: Perpetual down-and-out call (knock-out constant)
nodes.statement: $f(S) = S - bE\,(S/(bE))^{-\gamma}$, $\gamma = 2r/\sigma^2$. The discount $bE(S/bE)^{-\gamma}$ has elasticity $> 1$ (levered), and $f$ is concave in $S$.

nodes.name: Perpetual callable warrant value
nodes.statement: $F(S) = \left(\dfrac{K}{K+E}\right) E\,S$, with optimal call boundary $\bar{S} = K + E$ and call-provision value $C(S) = \left(\dfrac{E}{K+E}\right) S$.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (Lower bound on European warrant)
nodes.statement: If the exercise price of a European warrant is $E$ and no payouts are made to the common stock over the life of the warrant (or the warrant is protected against such payments), then $f(S,\tau;E) \geq \max[0, S - E P(\tau)]$.
assumptions: No payouts on the stock over the life of the warrant (or warrant is payout-protected)

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (No premature exercise)
nodes.statement: If the hypothesized conditions for Theorem 1 hold, an American warrant will never be exercised prior to expiration, and hence has the same value as a European warrant.
conclusions: $F(S,\tau;E) = f(S,\tau;E)$ and the option is never exercised early.

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (Perpetual warrant equals stock)
nodes.statement: If the hypothesized conditions for Theorem 1 hold, the value of a perpetual ($\tau \to \infty$) warrant must equal the value of the common stock.

nodes.name: Theorem 4 (Convexity in exercise price)
nodes.statement: If $F(S,\tau;E)$ is a rationally determined warrant price, then $F$ is a convex function of its exercise price $E$.

nodes.name: Theorem 5 (Lipschitz bound in exercise price)
nodes.statement: For European warrant $f$, if $E_1 < E_2$ then $-P(\tau)(E_2 - E_1) \leq f(S,\tau;E_2) - f(S,\tau;E_1) \leq 0$, and if $f$ is differentiable in $E$, $-P(\tau) \leq \partial f/\partial E \leq 0$.
assumptions: $f$ is the rational European warrant price

nodes.name: Theorem 6 (Scale homogeneity)
nodes.statement: If $k > 0$ is constant, $Q(t) = k S(t)$, $E_Q = k E$, then $F_Q(Q,\tau;E_Q) = k F(S,\tau;E)$ for all $S, \tau, E$ and each $k$.
assumptions: Linear scaling $Q = k S$, $E_Q = k E$
Same firm / same return distribution per dollar

nodes.name: Theorem 7 (Warrant on a portfolio bounded above by portfolio of warrants)
nodes.statement: If stocks $i=1,\dots,n$ have $S_i = S$ and the $(n+1)$st return is $Z_{n+1}(\tau) = \sum_i \lambda_i Z_i(\tau)$ with $\lambda_i \in [0,1]$, $\sum \lambda_i = 1$, then $F_{n+1}(S,\tau;E) \leq \sum_i \lambda_i F_i(S,\tau;E)$.

nodes.name: Corollary to Theorem 7 (Diversification hurts warrants)
nodes.statement: If, in addition, the $z_i(t)$ are identically distributed, then $F_{n+1}(S,\tau;E) \leq F_i(S,\tau;E)$ for $i=1,\dots,n$.

nodes.name: Theorem 8 (Warrant price increases with riskiness)
nodes.statement: The rationally determined warrant price is a non-decreasing function of the riskiness of its associated common stock (in the Rothschild-Stiglitz sense).
assumptions: Riskiness defined as a mean-preserving spread
conclusions: Warrant price is non-decreasing in stock riskiness.

nodes.name: Theorem 9 (Homogeneity in $S$ and $E$ under D.I.S.P.)
nodes.statement: If the distribution of returns per dollar invested in the common stock is independent of the level of the stock price (D.I.S.P.), then $F(S,\tau;E)$ is homogeneous of degree one in stock price and exercise price.
assumptions: D.I.S.P.: return distribution independent of stock-price level

nodes.name: Theorem 10 (Convexity in stock price under D.I.S.P.)
nodes.statement: If the distribution of returns per dollar invested in the common stock is independent of the stock-price level, then $F(S,\tau;E)$ is a convex function of $S$.

nodes.name: Theorem 11 (Stock-split / payout protection)
nodes.statement: If total return per dollar is invariant to the payout fraction and, on each ex-payout date, the number of shares purchasable for total $E$ dollars is increased by $(d/S_x)\%$ where $d$ is the payout and $S_x$ is the ex-payout share price, then the warrant is payout protected.
assumptions: Total return per dollar invariant to payout fraction
Adjustment rule: number of shares scaled by $1 + d/S_x$

nodes.name: Corollary to Theorem 11 (Equivalent exercise-price adjustment)
nodes.statement: If, on each ex-payout date, each warrant to purchase one share for $E$ is exchanged for $\lambda(=1 + d/S_x)$ warrants to purchase one share for $E/\lambda$, the warrant is payout protected.

nodes.name: Corollary on perpetual warrants with finite exercise-price changes
nodes.statement: If there is a finite number of changes in the exercise price of a payout-protected perpetual warrant, then it will not be exercised and its price equals the common-stock price.
conclusions: $F(S,\infty;\cdot) = S$ and the warrant is never exercised.

nodes.name: Theorem 12 (European put-call parity)
nodes.statement: If Assumption 1 holds and the borrowing and lending rates are equal ($P'(\tau) = P(\tau)$), then $g(S,\tau;E) = f(S,\tau;E) - S + E P(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Corollary 1 to Theorem 12 (Upper bound on European put)
nodes.statement: $E P(\tau) \geq g(S,\tau;E)$.
conclusions: European put value bounded above by present value of $E$.

nodes.name: Corollary 2 to Theorem 12 (Perpetual European put has zero value)
nodes.statement: The value of a perpetual ($\tau = \infty$) European put option is zero.

nodes.name: Theorem 13 (American put strictly exceeds European put)
nodes.statement: If for some $T < \tau$ there is a positive probability that $f(S,T;E) < E[1 - P(T)]$, then there is a positive probability that a $\tau$-year American put option will be exercised prematurely, and the American put value strictly exceeds its European counterpart.
conclusions: $G(S,\tau;E) > g(S,\tau;E)$, with positive probability of early exercise.

nodes.name: Theorem 14 (Warrant decreasing in $P(\tau)$, increasing in interest rate)
nodes.statement: For a given stock price, the warrant price is a non-increasing function of $P(\tau)$, and hence a non-decreasing function of the $\tau$-year interest rate.
conclusions: $\partial H/\partial P \leq 0$, equivalently warrant price non-decreasing in interest rate.

nodes.name: Theorem 15 (Warrant non-decreasing in variance)
nodes.statement: The warrant price is a non-decreasing function of the variance of the stock-price return.

nodes.name: Variance is a valid risk measure in the BSM model (Appendix 2)
nodes.statement: In the Black-Scholes-Merton log-normal model, increasing the variance $\sigma^2$ corresponds to a Rothschild-Stiglitz mean-preserving spread, so variance is a consistent measure of risk for warrant pricing.
conclusions: Higher $\sigma^2$ implies higher (or equal) warrant value via mean-preserving spread.

nodes.name: Counterexample showing D.I.S.P. is needed for Theorems 9, 10
nodes.statement: There exists a one-period European warrant pricing model with explicit uniform-distribution example $W(S,\lambda) = K[E^2/(4S) - 3E/2 + 9S/4 + \lambda^2 g(S)^2 S/12]$ that is not homogeneous of degree one in $(S,E)$ and can be locally concave in $S$, demonstrating that without D.I.S.P. Theorems 9 and 10 fail.
assumptions: Per-dollar return distribution depends on $S$ via $g(S)$

nodes.name: Rational option pricing problem
nodes.statement: Determine the price function $F(S,\tau;E)$ (or $f, G, g$) of an option such that the price is consistent with no-dominance and (later) no-arbitrage and yields explicit formulas under additional structural assumptions (BSM).

nodes.name: American put valuation
nodes.statement: Determine $G(S,\tau;E)$ solving $\tfrac12\sigma^2 S^2 G_{11} + r S G_1 - r G - G_2 = 0$ with $G(\infty,\tau;E)=0$, $G(S,0;E)=\max[0,E-S]$, and the obstacle constraint $G(S,\tau;E) \geq \max[0,E-S]$.

nodes.name: Down-and-out call valuation
nodes.statement: Find $f(S,T;E)$ satisfying the Black-Scholes PDE on $\{S > B(T)\}$ with $f(B[T],T;E)=0$, $f(S,0;E)=\max[0,S-E]$, where $B(T) = bE\exp[-\eta T]$.

nodes.name: Callable warrant valuation
nodes.statement: Find $F(S,\tau;E)$ for the callable warrant with company-chosen call boundary $\bar S$ minimizing $F$, plus issuer call price $K$, exercise payoff $\max[K, S-E]$ at the boundary, satisfying the BS PDE inside $0<S<\bar S$.

nodes.name: Modified European warrant valuation under exercise-price changes
nodes.statement: Dynamic-programming-style scheme that values a warrant with exercise-price schedule $E_0,E_1,\dots,E_n$ by solving European problems on each interval and stitching them via boundary conditions $F_j(S,\tau_j;E_j) = \max[0, S-E_j, F_{j-1}(S,\tau_j;E_{j-1})]$.
input: Stock-price process and pricing model for the European subproblem
output: American warrant value $F(S,\tau;E_0,\dots,E_n)$ at the current date

nodes.name: Black-Scholes-Merton PDE construction (alternative derivation)
nodes.statement: Form a zero-net-investment portfolio in the stock, the option, and a discount bond whose maturity matches the option, choose weights to eliminate $dz$ and $dq$ exposures, impose zero expected return, and combine to derive the parabolic PDE EP370.5 for $H(S,P,\tau;E)$.
input: Stock SDE EP370.3, bond SDE EP370.4
output: Parabolic PDE EP370.5 for $H$ with terminal/boundary conditions $H(0,P,\tau;E)=0$, $H(S,1,0;E)=\max[0,S-E]$, leading after change of variables to the heat equation and the BSM closed form (38)/(40).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 (dominance argument)
nodes.statement: Compare portfolio A (warrant + $E$ bonds) versus portfolio B (one share). Show A dominates B unless $f(S,\tau;E) + E P(\tau) \geq S$, giving the bound.

nodes.name: Construct comparison portfolios
nodes.statement: Let A = (warrant for $f(S,\tau;E)$) + ($E$ discount bonds at $P(\tau)$ each). Let B = one share at price $S$.

nodes.name: Compare terminal payoffs
nodes.statement: At expiration, B is worth $S^*$. Portfolio A is worth $E$ if $S^* \leq E$ and $S^*$ if $S^* > E$, so A's terminal value $\geq$ B's in every state.

nodes.name: Apply no-dominance
nodes.statement: By Assumption 1, current value of A must satisfy $f(S,\tau;E) + E P(\tau) \geq S$, hence $f(S,\tau;E) \geq \max[0, S - E P(\tau)]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Exercising yields $\max[0,S-E]$. By Theorem 1, $F \geq \max[0, S - E P(\tau)] > \max[0,S-E]$ for $\tau > 0$ since $P(\tau) < 1$. So the warrant is always worth more 'alive' than 'dead.'

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: From Theorem 1, $F(S,\infty;E) \geq \max[0, S - E P(\infty)] = S$ since $P(\infty) = 0$. Combined with $S \geq F(S,\tau;E)$ from (7), $F(S,\infty;E) = S$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4 (convexity in $E$)
nodes.statement: Compare a portfolio of $\lambda$ warrants at $E_1$ plus $(1-\lambda)$ at $E_2$ versus one warrant at $E_3 = \lambda E_1 + (1-\lambda) E_2$. By convexity of $\max[0,S^*-E]$ in $E$, the first dominates the second; no-dominance gives convexity of $F$ in $E$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7 (warrant on portfolio < portfolio of warrants)
nodes.statement: Let A hold $\lambda_i$ warrants on stock $i$, and B hold one warrant on the synthetic stock with returns $Z_{n+1} = \sum_i \lambda_i Z_i$. By convexity of $\max[0, S - E]$, A's terminal payoff $\geq$ B's pointwise; no-dominance yields $F_{n+1} \leq \sum_i \lambda_i F_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8 via large numbers
nodes.statement: Form $Z_{n+1}(\tau) = Z(\tau) + \tfrac1n \sum \epsilon_i$, average of i.i.d. mean-preserving-spread copies. By the corollary to Theorem 7, $F_{n+1}(S,\tau;E) \leq F_i(S,\tau;E)$. Letting $n\to\infty$, $Z_{n+1} \to Z$ in probability, so $F_z(S,\tau;E) \leq F_i(S,\tau;E)$, proving monotonicity in riskiness.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12 (put-call parity)
nodes.statement: Two zero-cost portfolios (long stock + long put + borrow $E P'(\tau)$ vs. long call + short stock + lend $E P(\tau)$) replicate call and put payoffs respectively. No-dominance gives both inequalities (15) and (16); when $P'(\tau)=P(\tau)$ they combine to equality $g = f - S + E P(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 13
nodes.statement: It suffices to find a state where $g(S^*,T;E) < G(S^*,T;E)$. From put-call parity, $g(S^*,T;E) = f(S^*,T;E) - S^* + E P(T)$. From (17), $G(S^*,T;E) \geq E - S^*$. The hypothesis $f(S^*,T;E) < E[1-P(T)]$ implies $g < G$, hence American > European with positive early-exercise probability.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 14 (warrant decreasing in $P$)
nodes.statement: $H$ is convex in $S$ and passes through the origin, so $H - S H_1 \leq 0$. From homogeneity (31), $H - S H_1 = P H_2$. Since $P > 0$, $H_2 \leq 0$. Because $P(\tau)$ is decreasing in the interest rate, the warrant is non-decreasing in the rate.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 15
nodes.statement: From (38) the variance enters $H$ only through $T = \int_0^\tau V^2(s)\,ds$. Differentiating, $\partial H / \partial \sigma^2$ is proportional to $y_2$, and $y_2 \geq 0$ since $y$ is the price of a legitimate American warrant, non-decreasing in time-to-expiry.

nodes.name: Posit $H(S,P,\tau;E)$ smooth and apply Ito
nodes.statement: Assume option price depends on $(S,P,\tau)$. Apply Ito's lemma using $(dS)^2=\sigma^2 S^2 dt$, $(dP)^2=\delta^2 P^2 dt$, $(dS\,dP)=\rho\sigma\delta SP\,dt$ to derive $dH$ as in eq. (25).

nodes.name: Form zero-net-investment portfolio in $(S,H,P)$
nodes.statement: Let $W_1, W_2, W_3$ be dollar holdings in stock, option, bond with $W_1 + W_2 + W_3 = 0$. Express $dY$ as a linear combination of $dt, dz, dq$.

nodes.name: Eliminate stochastic exposure
nodes.statement: Choose $W_i^*$ to zero coefficients of $dz$ and $dq$. The resulting $3\times 2$ system (28) admits a non-trivial solution iff the proportionality (29) holds among $(\beta-\mu)/(\delta-\mu)$, $-\gamma/\sigma$, etc.

nodes.name: Derive the parabolic PDE
nodes.statement: Combine (29) with the Ito form of $dH$ to obtain $\tfrac12[\sigma^2 S^2 H_{11} + 2\rho\sigma\delta SP H_{12} + \delta^2 P^2 H_{22}] - H_3 = 0$ (EP370.5).

nodes.name: Reduce to heat equation and solve
nodes.statement: Use $h(x,\tau)=H(S,P,\tau;E)/(EP)$ with $x=S/(EP(\tau))$ to reduce to $\tfrac12 V^2 x^2 h_{11} - h_2 = 0$, then change time to $T = \int_0^\tau V^2(s)\,ds$ and substitute $Z=\log x + T/2$, $\phi(Z,T) = y(x,T)/x$ to reach the canonical heat equation $\phi_2 = \tfrac12 \phi_{11}$.

nodes.name: Recover Black-Scholes-Merton formula
nodes.statement: Solve the heat equation by separation of variables / Fourier transform; invert the substitutions to obtain $H(S,P,\tau;E) = E P(\tau)\, y[S/(E P(\tau)), \int_0^\tau V^2(s)\,ds]$, recovering EP370.6 when $P(\tau)=e^{-r\tau}$ and $V^2 = \sigma^2$.

nodes.name: BSM formula independent of expected return $\alpha$
nodes.statement: The price (21) does not depend on the expected return on the stock, on risk preferences, or on aggregate supplies; it depends only on observables ($r$, $\sigma^2$). Hence option prices cannot be used to infer expected returns.

nodes.name: Necessary, not sufficient, role of CAPM
nodes.statement: Capital Asset Pricing Model is a sufficient but not necessary assumption for the BSM formula. The only piece of CAPM actually used is the no-sure-thing-profits condition (29).

nodes.name: Discrete-time Samuelson recursion is the correct one
nodes.statement: When dividends and exercise-price changes occur on discrete dates, premature exercise can occur only at those dates. Samuelson's discrete recursion with intervals matched to those dates is the correct formulation; the continuous-time PDE is the approximation.

nodes.name: Closed-form American put for finite $\tau$
nodes.statement: No closed-form solution to the American put PDE (EP370.9) is known for finite $\tau$; only the perpetual case admits an explicit solution. Solutions for finite $\tau$ require numerical methods.

nodes.name: Application to corporate liabilities and term structure
nodes.statement: Develop a theory of risk-structure of interest rates and term structure of interest rates by treating the firm's value as the basic security and individual liabilities (debt, convertible bonds, equity) as contingent claims, along Cootner-Merton lines.

nodes.name: Proportional dividend $D = pS$ (perpetual warrant)
nodes.statement: With $D(S,\tau) = pS$, $p > 0$, the European warrant is $W = e^{-p\tau} S \Phi(d_1) - E e^{-r\tau} \Phi(d_2)$, premature exercise can occur, and the perpetual American warrant solution is a power function tangent to $S - E$ (Samuelson-McKean).

nodes.name: Constant dividend $D = d$ (perpetual warrant)
nodes.statement: With $D = d$ constant and $E > d/r$, the perpetual warrant is $W(S,\infty;E) = (d/r)\,(2d/(\sigma^2 S))^{2r/\sigma^2} M(2r/\sigma^2, 2 + 2r/\sigma^2 - 2d/\sigma^2, \cdot)$ where $M$ is the confluent hypergeometric function (Figure 2).

nodes.name: Continuously changing exercise price $E(\tau)$
nodes.statement: If $E(\tau)$ is differentiable and decreasing in $\tau$, the warrant satisfies the BS PDE with effective rate $\eta(\tau) = r - \dot E/E$. When $\int_0^\tau \eta(s)\,ds \geq 0$ (i.e., $E(\tau) \geq E(0)\,e^{-r\tau}$), no premature exercise; the value matches a fixed-strike $E(0)$ warrant under rate $r$.
